passage: Keerthana, sit with me a minute. Your Paati was nineteen once, you know. In the hostel they called me Nimmi, because Nirmala was too long to shout down a corridor. There was a boy in our chemistry batch, Mohan, who could make the whole lab laugh when a burette leaked, and who answered the professor without a single stammer. We spoke perhaps four times, near the cycle stand, about nothing much. By the fourth time I had already planned our house by the river and decided he loved old film songs the way I did. He never once mentioned songs, kutty. I painted the empty spaces with my own colours. At night I wrote his name in the margins of my notes and felt dizzy with it. Only much later did I wonder who he really was, under all my paint.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala and Mohan talk?
qa.a: They spoke perhaps four times, near the cycle stand, about nothing much.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she planned a house by the river after only four talks?
qa.a: She felt giddy and excited, so thrilled by Mohan's humour and confidence that she filled every unknown with her own hopes, like his love of film songs.

qa.q: At this stage, what could the young Nirmala have done before building a whole future around Mohan?
qa.a: She could have enjoyed the attraction while getting to know him slowly, asking what he actually liked instead of deciding he loved her film songs.

qa.q: How might Mohan have seen those few talks by the cycle stand?
qa.a: To Mohan they were probably light, friendly chats with a batchmate; he likely had no idea she had already imagined a house by the river.

grounding: Shows a student drawn to a classmate's humour and confidence who imagines a whole future, and his tastes, from only a few conversations.

passage: The hostel lights died at nine, and Abhay's phone showed six percent. Of course it did. An hour earlier, after deleting it three times, he had finally sent Nandini: "There's a new chai place near the library. Saturday?" Before that he had only replied to her stories, a clapping reaction on her sketch, a "haha" on her burnt noodles. Now the word Seen sat under his message and nothing else. He dimmed the screen to save battery and kept waking it anyway. Four minutes. Eleven. Last time she had answered in two minutes; did the gap mean something? His roommate snored. At five percent the phone buzzed: "Saturday works! Can we make it 5? I have lab till 4 😊" Abhay read it five times by torchlight, grinning in the dark, and did not dare use the last of the battery to reply properly.

qa.q: How much battery did Abhay's phone show when the hostel lights went out?
qa.a: It showed six percent when the hostel lights died at nine.

qa.q: Why did Abhay keep waking his screen even though the battery was low?
qa.a: He was anxious and afraid of being turned down, so every minute without Nandini's reply felt huge and he could not stop checking.

qa.q: What could help Abhay at this uncertain stage, before he reads meaning into the next delay?
qa.a: He could remind himself that a slow reply usually means someone is busy, and put the phone away for a while instead of treating each gap as a verdict.

qa.q: How might Nandini see the invitation when she finally replies?
qa.a: Nandini seems pleased, even suggesting a time, and is probably unaware that her eleven minutes of silence felt enormous to Abhay.

grounding: Shows a young man who has started replying to stories and suggesting chai, with fear of rejection making reply speed feel huge.

subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]
passage: You asked how I knew, Shreya, so your Tanuja Masi will tell you. At twenty I was seeing Vivek from the debate club. The first months were long walks and his clever lines. Then we began meeting every day. I saw that he sulked a whole evening if he lost an argument. I saw him keep a waiter standing while he joked with me, never once saying thank you. And when I told him I wanted to work in a village clinic after college, he laughed and said, "You'll grow out of that." The glow did not vanish in one day; it thinned, like a dupatta washed too often. One night, walking home, I stopped asking whether I liked being with him and started asking whether I liked him. That is a harder question, my dear. It took me three more weeks to answer it honestly.

qa.q: What did Vivek say when Tanuja mentioned working in a village clinic?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "You'll grow out of that."

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel as she kept noticing Vivek's sulking and his manner with the waiter?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and quietly disappointed, as the early glow thinned and she saw habits and values that clashed with her own.

qa.q: What turning point does Tanuja reach on that walk home, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She stops asking whether she likes the feeling and asks whether she likes Vivek himself, which lets her judge the real person rather than the early excitement.

qa.q: What would change if Vivek had taken the clinic plan seriously instead of laughing?
qa.a: Tanuja might have felt respected in what she valued, and her harder question could have had a warmer answer, though his sulking and rudeness would still need weighing.

grounding: Shows the early glow fading as a young woman meets her partner often and sees his habits, moods and values more clearly.

passage: The laundromat on Queen Street smelled of warm cotton and cheap soap. Bao watched her socks tumble and made herself say it before the dryer stopped. "Abebe, we've been seeing each other for six weeks. I'd like us to be exclusive. Where do you stand?" He looked up from folding a towel, eyebrows high. For a long second only the machines spoke. Bao's heart hammered; she had rehearsed this on the tram and still her voice wobbled at the end. "I was hoping you'd ask," he said slowly, "because I was scared to. Yes. I'd like that." She laughed, mostly from relief. "I was ready for a no, you know. I just couldn't keep guessing every time you didn't text back." He handed her the warm towel. "No more guessing, then."

qa.q: Where was Bao when she asked Abebe where he stood?
qa.a: She was at the laundromat on Queen Street, watching her socks tumble in the dryer.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling in the long second before Abebe answered?
qa.a: She was nervous and scared of a no; her heart hammered and her voice wobbled, and then she laughed with relief.

qa.q: Why did asking directly work better for Bao than waiting?
qa.a: It risked a no, but it ended the guessing over unanswered texts, so both of them could act on a clear answer.

qa.q: How does Abebe experience Bao's question?
qa.a: Abebe is relieved and glad, because he had wanted the same thing but had been too scared to ask it himself.

grounding: Shows one partner asking directly about exclusivity, accepting the risk of a no in exchange for an end to weeks of guessing.

passage: Coach's notebook, Thursday. Uma and Vijay stayed back after rehearsal again, and I overheard more than I meant to. Last Sunday Uma ate lunch at Vijay's home for the first time. She told me she had practised eating fish curry with her fingers so nobody would think her fussy, and that his cousins teased her Tamil accent kindly. This week it was Vijay's turn: he sat through her grandmother's questions about his surname and his family's church. What struck me was not the questions but how the two of them answered. When Uma's aunt asked, "And where will you live, whose festivals will you keep?", Vijay looked at Uma before replying, and she said, "We are still working that out together." Both looked tired tonight. I told them the green room is free on Fridays if they want a quiet place to talk, and I will keep checking in.

qa.q: What did Uma practise before lunch at Vijay's home?
qa.a: She practised eating fish curry with her fingers so nobody would think her fussy.

qa.q: What does the coach seem to feel while watching Uma and Vijay after rehearsal?
qa.a: The coach seems concerned about how tired they look and also impressed by how they answer the family's questions as a pair.

qa.q: What support could help the couple at this stage of meeting families?
qa.a: A quiet place to agree on their answers in private, like the green room the coach offered, helps them face questions about home and festivals as a team.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay when Uma's grandmother asks about his surname and his family's church?
qa.a: It is probably tense and exposing to be judged on his background, though looking to Uma before replying shows he wants them to answer together.

grounding: Shows an onlooker noticing a young couple adjusting to each other's food, families and questions of faith and household, and facing them together.

passage: On the balcony of their rented flat in Pune, Rekha set down two glasses of cutting chai and a sheet of paper. "Before we say forever, let's be boring and honest," she said. Shreya laughed, but she took the pen. They had been together two years. Shreya had seen Rekha snap at everyone during her father's surgery, then go back and apologise to each nurse by name. Rekha had seen Shreya lose her job and spend a week in pyjamas before sending out forty applications. They had also danced badly at three weddings. On the paper they wrote: Rekha wants to study abroad in two years. Shreya wants to stay near her mother. How we share rent. Who calls whom first after a fight. They circled the abroad question twice and agreed to decide it together by spring. Then Shreya put the pen down. "I'm choosing you, knowing all of this." Rekha squeezed her hand. "Same. Eyes open."

qa.q: How long had Shreya and Rekha been together?
qa.a: They had been together two years.

qa.q: What does Rekha's suggestion to be 'boring and honest' suggest she wants?
qa.a: She wants their promise to rest on clear, shared facts rather than on the joy of the moment, and she seems calm and secure enough to face hard topics.

qa.q: What makes this a strong moment to commit rather than an impulsive one?
qa.a: They have already seen each other at their worst, during the surgery and the job loss, and they name real goals, even the clash over studying abroad, before deciding.

qa.q: What would change if Shreya had said 'forever' without talking about Rekha's plan to study abroad?
qa.a: The clash with Shreya's wish to stay near her mother would likely surface later as a painful surprise, instead of being something they agreed to work on together.

grounding: Shows a couple committing only after seeing each other through stress and joy and talking honestly about goals.

passage:
"So Nirmala Aunty told you I'm a data analyst who reads too much?" Alka asked.
"She said you'd grill me," Sameer grinned. "Go on."
"Fine. You're in Bengaluru. My job is in Pune and I just got promoted. Would you move, or would I be expected to?"
"Honestly? I don't know yet. I like my team. But I wouldn't expect you to move just because you're the woman."
Alka laughed, then caught herself enjoying it a little too much. "And children? My mother already has names picked."
"Mine too," he said. "Not before thirty, for me. Is that a problem?"
"No. It's actually a relief." She stirred her coffee. "I'm having fun. That's what worries me."
"Why?"
"Because fun is easy. City, career, being ready, those are the hard parts."
"Then let's meet again," Sameer said, "and talk about the hard parts properly."

qa.q: Where is Alka's job?
qa.a: Alka's job is in Pune, where she just got promoted.

qa.q: Why does Alka say that having fun is what worries her?
qa.a: She is excited by Sameer's company but cautious, afraid that the easy fun might hide the hard questions about city, career and being ready.

qa.q: What is a wise next step for Alka at this early stage?
qa.a: Meeting again, as Sameer suggests, while keeping the practical questions on the table, lets her test the spark against real plans instead of one pleasant evening.

qa.q: How might Sameer be feeling when Alka asks whether he would move?
qa.a: He may feel put on the spot but also respected, since he answers honestly that he does not know yet and seems to enjoy her directness.

grounding: Shows a young professional introduced through family feeling real attraction alongside careful questions about career, city and readiness.

passage:
Monday. Pradeep's phone lit up at 7:10 a.m.: "Good morning. Big client call today, you've got this 👍" It was from Chetan. They had been seeing each other a month, and the texts now ran from breakfast to bedtime.
Thursday. Pradeep came home from the office too tired to cook. Chetan arrived with dal and rice in a steel tiffin and stayed to wash up. They sketched out Saturday: the flea market, then chai on a friend's terrace. Pradeep noticed he had stopped rehearsing what to say around him.
The next Tuesday. Pradeep was buried in a project report he had half forgotten. At 9 p.m. Chetan texted: "Wasn't your report due tomorrow? Want me to read it over?" Pradeep stared at the screen. Nobody had ever kept track of his deadline for him before. Flowers would have been nice. This was better.

qa.q: What did Chetan bring on Thursday?
qa.a: He arrived with dal and rice in a steel tiffin and stayed to wash up.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Chetan remembered his report deadline?
qa.a: He felt touched and cared for, moved that someone had kept track of his deadline for him, which meant more to him than flowers would.

qa.q: What small habit could help this closeness keep growing?
qa.a: Both could keep noticing and doing small reliable things, like checking on each other's deadlines or turning up with food on tired evenings.

qa.q: How might Chetan experience these weeks with Pradeep?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels welcome and settled, since his morning texts and tiffin visits are received gladly and their weekends are now planned together.

grounding: Shows a new couple's daily texts, shared meals and weekend plans, and how a small act of dependability means more than a grand gesture.

passage:
The argument started over a calendar. Rafael had written "Mãe, lunch" on every Sunday until December, the way it had always been in his family. Liam saw it on the fridge of their small Lisbon flat and went quiet.
"Every Sunday?"
"It's lunch. It's family."
"It's the only day we both have off."
Rafael felt his face go hot. He had expected Liam to love those loud, crowded tables. Instead Liam said, carefully, "I like your mum. I just thought we'd decide our weekends together."
Rafael wanted to slam the cupboard. He didn't. He sat down, rubbed his eyes and said, "I didn't even know that was a question for us."
Liam half smiled. "Maybe that's the real question."
They didn't settle it that night, but neither of them left the table, and Rafael noticed that mattered more to him than winning.

qa.q: What had Rafael written on every Sunday until December?
qa.a: He had written "Mãe, lunch" on every Sunday until December.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when Liam questioned the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defensive, with his face going hot and an urge to slam the cupboard, because he had expected Liam to love those family lunches.

qa.q: What did Rafael choose at the turning point, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He sat down instead of slamming the cupboard and admitted he hadn't seen weekends as a shared decision, which kept the talk open for another day.

qa.q: How does Liam see the calendar on the fridge?
qa.a: To Liam it looks as if their only shared day off was decided without him, so he wants a say, not a rejection of Rafael's family.

grounding: Shows a couple's first real disagreement, over time with family, revealing different expectations and how each behaves under strain.

subtype: Stage 4: Fear of loss of freedom [Actor]
passage:
In the tailoring shop by Sirsa's bus stand, Sarita pinned a blouse and missed the pin twice. Nikita, stitching at the next machine, noticed. For a week Sarita had been quiet, ever since Hemant's mother began talking about which room would be theirs after the wedding in March.
"You love him, na?" Nikita asked.
"I do. That's the trouble," Sarita said. "I love him, and I also keep thinking of this shop, my late evenings, my own key. It feels like a door shutting slowly."
That evening, when Hemant rang, she almost said, "All fine." Instead she said, "Can I tell you something that scares me, before March and not after?"
There was a pause on the line. Then Hemant said, "Tell me. I'd rather know now."

qa.q: What had Hemant's mother begun talking about?
qa.a: She had begun talking about which room would be theirs after the wedding in March.

qa.q: How can you tell Sarita feels torn about the move?
qa.a: She misses the pin twice and has been quiet for a week; she says she loves Hemant yet fears losing her shop, her late evenings and her own key, so she feels torn and scared.

qa.q: What turning point does Sarita choose, and why is it kinder?
qa.a: She tells Hemant her fear before March instead of saying "All fine", so they can face it together rather than discover it after the wedding.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita, stitching beside Sarita this week?
qa.a: Nikita sees Sarita's silence and clumsy pinning and seems concerned enough to ask gently, giving her a safe first place to say what she feels.

grounding: Shows a young woman growing quiet as living together nears, feeling both love and a closing door, and choosing to say it early.
